_comment: WHAT A CHANGE TO EACH RESOURCE COSTS A RUNNING DEPLOYMENT.
Terraform's own plan says create / update / replace / destroy. It cannot say
which of those stops a machine that is running somebody's build, because it
does not know that billet is on these hosts — ADR-004 keeps live nodes outside
Terraform deliberately. This table is that missing half, and scripts/tfclassify
joins it to `terraform show -json` so a plan can be read before it is applied.
THE CLASS DESCRIBES THE WORST ORDINARY CHANGE to the resource, not the change
in front of you: tfclassify takes the worse of this class and what the plan's
own actions imply, so a destroy is treated as destructive whatever is written
here. Erring high costs an operator a drain they did not need; erring low costs
somebody's build, and only one of those is recoverable.
in_place    nothing running is disturbed.
replacement the resource is recreated. No running job is on it, but there is
a window where it does not exist.
draining    a host that may be running jobs stops, or loses something a
running job depends on. billet's durable drain comes first, and
a Terraform timeout is not permission to terminate a job.
destructive data does not come back.
EVERY MANAGED RESOURCE IN EVERY MODULE MUST HAVE AN ENTRY, and tfclass's own
test refuses a missing one — a plan reader silent about a resource it has
never heard of is a gate that passes without examining it.
Keyed by type.name rather than by full address, because the same resource
means the same thing in whichever module declares it: the node role exists in
both fleet-ec2 and fleet-codebuild and is the identity a running instance or
build carries either way.

aws_instance.control_plane.reason: the controller itself. Replacing it stops the process that is polling GitHub, holding the capacity ledger and dispatching to every node.

aws_volume_attachment.ledger.reason: detaching stops the instance first (stop_instance_before_detaching), so this is a controller outage wearing a storage change's clothes.

aws_ebs_volume.ledger.reason: the SQLite ledger, the deployment identity and the node-wire CA. prevent_destroy already fails the plan closed; a resize or a cross-AZ move is what gets here.
aws_ebs_volume.ledger.remedy: billet local backup, then restore onto the replacement

aws_cloudwatch_metric_alarm.control_plan.reason: the EC2 auto-recovery alarm. Changing it alters what happens to a FUTURE hardware failure and disturbs nothing now.

aws_security_group.control_plane.reason: replacing it detaches the group the running controller's node wire and cache endpoint are reachable on, so every node loses its control plane.

aws_security_group.runner.reason: replacing it severs the network of every instance already running a job in it.

aws_vpc_security_group_ingress_rule.node.reason: a port or CIDR change recreates the rule, so the node wire is briefly unreachable. Nodes redial; nothing running is destroyed.
the enrollment port, which is shut in the steady state and used only while a machine is being added.

aws_vpc_security_group_ingress_rule.ssh.reason: SSH for configuration management. billet does not use it.

aws_vpc_security_group_ingress_rule.cach.reason: the runners' path to the cache endpoint. The cache fails open to a miss, so a gap costs cache hits rather than jobs.

aws_vpc_security_group_egress_rule.contr.reason: the controller's only route to GitHub. Without it the control plane cannot poll, acquire, or report a job's completion.

aws_vpc_security_group_egress_rule.runne.reason: a running job's only route out. Recreating it mid-job fails checkouts and package installs in whatever is running.

aws_iam_role.this.reason: the standalone controller's own instance identity. Replacing it takes away the credentials the running controller is using.

aws_iam_instance_profile.this.reason: as above: the profile the running controller obtains its credentials through.

aws_iam_role.node.reason: the identity a running node uses to launch, reap and reach its cache. Replacing it strands compute the node can no longer account for.

aws_iam_instance_profile.node.reason: the profile that role reaches the node through.

aws_iam_role_policy.node.reason: an identity policy is evaluated PER REQUEST, not frozen when a session begins — so a narrowed grant lands on the launches, teardowns and registration writes billet is making for leases that are already open, and those failures are somebody's job.

aws_iam_role.build.reason: the service role a CodeBuild build runs under. Replacing it breaks builds already executing.

aws_iam_role_policy.build.reason: the identity a RUNNING BUILD is executing as, and an identity policy is evaluated per request rather than frozen at assume-time. An update landing after CodeBuild starts and before the build reads its staged registration leaves that job unable to register at all; one landing later revokes the log writes it is still making.

aws_iam_role.fleet.reason: the role a reserved CodeBuild fleet's instances run under.

aws_iam_role_policy.fleet.reason: the identity a reserved fleet's instances execute under, evaluated per request while a build is running on one.

aws_iam_role_policy.pass_role.reason: the node's PassRole grant. Without it RunInstances is refused — so an update landing between a lease being escrowed and its instance being launched fails that job rather than a later one.

aws_iam_role_policy.controller_sweep.reason: the controller's list-and-delete grant on the staged-registration path. It never touches a lease that is open: the sweep acts only on one the ledger has already closed and aged past ServiceInventoryWindow, so losing it during a window fails no job — it leaves the leaked registrations a dead node stranded in place until the grant is back, and the sweep is a retry loop that finds them on its next pass.

aws_iam_role_policy.backups.reason: the controller's get/put/list grant on its own archive prefix. Updated in place.

aws_iam_role_policy.builder.reason: the AMI builder's grant on the node role. `billet ami build` is an operator command run deliberately, not something a running job depends on, so removing it mid-flight fails the next build rather than a lease that is already open — and an identity policy is evaluated per request, so a build in progress would lose it too. Nothing on a host stops.

aws_iam_role_policy.spot.reason: the node's grant on the interruption queue. Losing it during a window costs the two-minute warning and therefore the ATTRIBUTION of a spot reclaim — but AWS takes that instance either way, so the job is lost by the reclaim rather than by this change.

aws_codebuild_project.this.reason: the project billet starts builds in, and half of what tells its own builds from somebody else's. Replacing it orphans every build already running in the old one.

aws_codebuild_fleet.this.reason: reserved capacity. AWS keeps a reserved instance alive between builds, so replacing the fleet takes the machines running jobs with it.

aws_cloudwatch_log_group.this.reason: destroying a log group deletes the build logs in it, which are the only record of why a job failed.

aws_cloudwatch_log_group.spot_router.reason: as above, for the spot router's own logs.

aws_kms_key.registrations.reason: the key CodeBuild runner registrations are encrypted with. A destroyed key makes its ciphertext permanently unreadable.

aws_kms_alias.registrations.reason: a name for the key. The key and its ciphertext are unaffected.

aws_kms_key.cache.reason: the key the cache's EBS volumes and snapshots are encrypted with; destroying it makes every existing snapshot unreadable.

aws_s3_bucket.cache.reason: the cache's atomic pointer, lease and fencing state. Losing it loses which snapshot each cache generation refers to.

aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block.cache.reason: weakening it exposes the bucket, which is worth a person's attention and disturbs nothing running.

aws_s3_bucket_server_side_encryption_con.reason: applies to objects written AFTER the change; existing objects keep the encryption they were written with.

aws_s3_bucket.backups.reason: the off-site copies of the ledger, the deployment identity, the GitHub App key and the node-wire CA. This bucket is the thing that survives losing the controller.

aws_s3_bucket_versioning.backups.reason: versioning is what makes a no-delete grant mean anything. Suspending it does not delete an archive today and removes the property that protects every archive tomorrow.

aws_s3_bucket_lifecycle_configuration.ba.reason: the retention rule. It expires NONCURRENT versions only; a rule that reached current objects would remove backups on a timer.

aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block.backup.reason: weakening it exposes two private keys and a ledger to the internet. Worth a person's attention; nothing running is disturbed.

aws_s3_bucket_server_side_encryption_con.reason: applies to archives written after the change.

aws_sqs_queue.interruptions.reason: billet requires a spot node's node.name to equal this queue's basename, so replacing it under a different name needs the node's config changed to match before it can read its own interruptions.
aws_sqs_queue.interruptions.remedy: update node.name to the new spot_node_name output

aws_sqs_queue.spot_nodes.reason: one further spot node's interruption queue, named exactly that node. A changed spot_node_names entry replaces the queue under a new name — one that node cannot read until its node.name matches — and a removed entry destroys it, which the plan reports as destructive whatever is written here.
aws_sqs_queue.spot_nodes.remedy: set that node's node.name to its key in the interruption_queue_urls output

aws_cloudwatch_event_rule.spot_interrupt.reason: the rule routing EC2 spot warnings to the queue. While it is absent a two-minute warning is missed and the job dies without billet recording why.

aws_cloudwatch_event_target.spot_router.reason: as above: the target the rule delivers to.

aws_lambda_function.spot_router.reason: the tag-scoped router between the event rule and the queue.

aws_lambda_permission.spot_router.reason: EventBridge's permission to invoke the router.

aws_iam_role.spot_router.reason: the router's own execution role. No job runs under it.

aws_cloudwatch_metric_alarm.spot_router_.reason: the router's error alarm. Changing it alters what an operator is told about a FUTURE failure and disturbs nothing running.

aws_vpc.this.reason: the network every host and every job instance is in. Replacing it replaces everything under it.

aws_subnet.this.reason: where the controller and every runner launch. Replacing it forces the controller to be replaced with it.

aws_internet_gateway.this.reason: the created network's only route out, which is a running job's path to GitHub.

aws_route_table.this.reason: as above: replacing it removes the default route while it is recreated.

aws_route_table_association.this.reason: what binds the subnet to that route table.

terraform_data.active_build_guard.reason: a plan-time guard rather than infrastructure. It refuses the apply it is part of; it changes nothing on a host.

aws_db_instance.ledger.reason: the capacity ledger itself on the PostgreSQL profile. Replacing it does not move the rows: every lease, node registration, custody record and rollout is in this database, and a controller that comes up against an empty one re-admits capacity that is already running somebody's build. deletion_protection and a mandatory final snapshot are what make the plan fail closed rather than this entry.
aws_db_instance.ledger.remedy: billet drain --wait, then restore from a snapshot deliberately — this is not a change to apply and watch

aws_db_parameter_group.ledger.reason: holds synchronous_commit = on, which billet checks at startup and refuses without. Its VALUE is dynamic and applies without a restart (measured: describe-engine-default-parameters reports ApplyType dynamic) — but attaching a DIFFERENT group to the instance is pending-reboot, and that reboot takes the controller's connection with it mid-transaction.

aws_db_subnet_group.ledger.reason: which subnets the ledger is reachable in. Changing it moves the endpoint the controller is connected to.

aws_security_group.ledger.reason: the only thing that admits the controller to its own ledger. Replacing it detaches the database from every rule referencing it, and a controller whose next write cannot reach PostgreSQL stops.

aws_vpc_security_group_ingress_rule.ledg.reason: the controller's permission to reach the ledger, by group identity. A window with no rule is a window with no ledger.

aws_iam_role_policy.state_secrets.reason: what lets the host read the ledger credential and assemble BILLET_STATE_DSN. IAM is evaluated per request rather than frozen when the role was assumed, so removing it takes effect on a running controller's next fetch — the same reason every other role policy here is draining rather than in_place.
